newsitem.title: USA: FORECAST - U.S durable goods seen rebounding in Sept.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST - U.S durable goods seen rebounding in Sept.

text.p: U.S. durable goods orders in September likely rebounded from a sharp decline in August, boosted partly by aircraft purchases, analysts said.
Economists polled by Reuters, on average, predicted September orders rose 2.0 percent overall and 1.3 percent without defense orders. August orders fell 3.2 percent and 3.6 percent, respectively.
The data are due to be released Friday, October 25 at 0830 EDT/1230 GMT.
"There were significant aircraft orders that should come through. That's going to really push up the overall number," said Evelina Tainer, chief economist at Indosuez Carr Futures.

The August decline in durable goods orders was the largest monthly drop since a 3.4 percent plunge in April 1995. Weaker orders for new aircraft and parts accounted for more than half the falloff in transportation goods. The only category that registered an increase that month was defense capital orders.
Analysts emphasized the data are among the most volatile of the widely watched statistics. Therefore, a bounce-back after such a steep plunge would not be unusual.
"Once you get a sizeable decline like this, it wouldn't be surprising to see a big rebound," said William Griggs, managing director at Griggs & Santow Inc.
Transportation equipment, which includes aircraft orders among others, is not the only sector expected to post an increase in September.
Robert McGee, chief economist at Tokai Bank Ltd, forecasted a rebound in most categories.
"The weakness was so widespread in the last number and it seemed to overstate what we think (is) happening in the factory sector," McGee said.
He noted that purchasing managers' reports still show orders growing. "So it makes sense that we would offset some of the weakness that we saw in August," he said.

For example, the National Association of Purchasing Management-Metro Detroit survey in September showed the latest readings on new orders and production activity strongly sugggest additional expansion in the coming months.
Indosuez's Tainer looked to the housing market for clues about the pace of durable goods orders.
"The housing market has maintained itself pretty well," Tainer said. "So we could see furniture and appliances pick up a little bit."
Analysts were also careful not to overstate the impact of any rebound in durables in September in light of the deep decline in the previous month.
"I don't think (a rebound) has a mammoth message," Griggs said. "...it's just a confirmation (of) how volatile the series continues to be."
